A dispatch from Kyiv

Even filling the tank has to wait

Terry Yiu’s posts describe an explosion outside the window, an attack on a medical centre the family had visited, and the difficulty of keeping a car ready to leave.

The car was at half a tank. Terry Yiu says the family normally fills it to be ready to escape at short notice, but the evening’s attempt in Kyiv ended without fuel: Two gas stations that we visited in Kyiv shut down in fear of being attacked.

Earlier, Yiu reported a massive explosion in central Kyiv outside their window, posting a video and saying it had happened thirty minutes before.

The subsequent post about Dobrobut brings the day back to an ordinary family errand. This was the medical facility where their son had recently had X-rays, and where they expected to arrange another visit.

In a reply, Yiu says the family plans to leave in about a month and is waiting for the child’s passports. These posts are a personal account of the day, with the practical preparations still unfinished.

Learning to make things

Teach the code, or teach the prompt?

Hodlbod has built a dungeon-crawler project for their son and now wonders whether teaching programming might feel, in retrospect, like teaching assembly in the nineteen-nineties.

The question to the network is direct: Are you teaching your kids to program, or prompt? The post is wary of handing a child an LLM before adults have worked out a healthy relationship with the tools. Hardware, philosophy and AI architecture all appear among the alternatives hodlbod is considering.

Cyphernomad’s contribution to the thread starts with Minecraft mods. Their children use them to put an understanding of computation into practice, and also use AI to configure systems and develop plugins.

Even within that household, the approaches differ: My oldest prefers to prompt and take it from there, my youngest prefers to code and only let the AI do the tedious, boring stuff.

Sonar · The old balance stays

Cashu moves in. Breez isn’t erased.

Vincenzo Palazzo describes Sonar’s move to a Cashu wallet on iOS and Android. New installations use Cashu; existing Breez wallets remain as legacy wallets, with funds left in place until the user moves them.

The public handle changes over only after a confirmed move. Palazzo says removal of the old wallet is offered after two synced checks find it empty, and stops if money arrives after the check. The migration is meant to preserve both the balance and the address other people already know.

The release also adds reactions inside encrypted chats and optional sharing of local time. In a separate explanation, Palazzo identifies 1.15.1 as the corrective build: 1.15.0 could open to an empty conversation list and repeatedly send local-time shares to groups. The fix repairs the local index on opening.

Dispatches

Breez SDK

Dollars in, a familiar balance out

Breez announces that its SDK can receive USDC and USDT from more than thirty networks, naming Ethereum, Base, Solana and Tron.

The incoming payment goes to a bitcoin or dollar balance. Breez pitches this as a way for app developers to accept those payments without integrating another chain, and points to Glow as a place to try it.

The announcement is about a new route for receiving payments. It does not give a fee schedule or a settlement-time guarantee.

Amber 6.6.6

One equals sign, one failed connection

Amber fixes a connection parser that corrupted values containing an equals sign, including secrets with base64 padding. Clients using NDK then rejected the altered secret.

The release also repairs hard-to-see controls in both themes. Feedback reports now use the relays advertised by Amber’s repository announcement, with a fallback if that announcement cannot be fetched.

Longer Tor timeouts give slow relays more time to confirm publication. A small release about getting the connection and its status right.

White Noise

The next contact is an agent

White Noise announces connectors for Claude, OpenClaw, Hermes, OpenCode, Pi and Codex, letting users message their AI agents from the same app as their human contacts.

There is also a boundary to the present group setup. Asked about custom relays per group, Max says: we haven't started working on this, first priority is to make it work great in controlled environment.

The connector announcement expands who can be reached through the app; relay choice within each group remains work ahead.

In brief

Blitz opens in the browser

Blitz Wallet announces its full wallet in a browser, with Bitcoin sending and receiving and no app installation required. The project says users keep the same keys and that it does not touch them.

Everything is 200 sats

BitcoinEkasi reports a busier thrift store, where every item is priced at 200 sats. The stated aim is to teach residents to use Bitcoin for everyday purchases.

A supporter experiment

Rabble describes Divine Supporters as one experiment in paying for the service’s servers and team while keeping funding aligned with users. More experiments are planned.
